conflicting_evidence.what_to_do: A conflict here is not a theory being wrong, which is what the rounds are for; it is a reason to doubt that the objective measures what it is named after. Do not settle it by preferring the source you started with. The round that settles it looks for a THIRD kind of evidence, or for a better instrument tested against the anchors you already hold — and either way both readings go in as rival theories so the next batch is chosen for what separates them.

measuring evenly BEFORE having a theory is the one thing a campaign cannot go back and do. In a controlled comparison on a real library, evidence chosen evenly gave belief posteriors that were right 67% of the time while asserting 0.77; evidence chosen to maximise the objective was right 23% while asserting 0.76. The arithmetic was the same in both — only the sampling differed.
to get an information-directed batch again, state a principle naming a factor this one does not — the space it can reason about is the space it can propose in.

program_countdown: 4 of the scored candidates carry a `program`. At 5 this stops enumerating and returns a breeding set instead — the best programs so far, the worst for contrast, and the factors on which the two groups differ, which is the material for writing a better one. 1 more to go. These programs carry no `holes`, and that is what keeps proposing on the breeding set: with nothing named inside a program there is no neighbourhood to enumerate, so the record hands back the best and the worst and asks you to write the next one yourself. Naming one hole changes that — a hole is a formula, so its edits are defined, generation varies one hole at a time, and a gain becomes attributable to a component instead of to a whole rewrite. The skeleton is usually something you looked up; the holes are what this campaign is actually searching.
